To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
firms contribute to public OSS code without being obliged to, and they do this selectively.
firms contribute a large share of their developments to public embedded Linux and that this openness is selective.
firms contribute many of their developments back to the public, and do so selectively, revealing about half of their developments.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the management of openness, a key issue in open innovation.
a novel phenomenon: firms that contribute their own developments to a public, open development process.
the question: Why do firms reveal their innovations in public, and how do they protect their intellectual property?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
openness is a viable option in the development of embedded Linux.
firms are not only willing to open up their product development processes, but they also do so.
open development is a feasible strategy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
openness is not an either-or issue.
openness is not an all or nothing phenomenon, but rather a matter of degree, with a wide variety of possible strategies.
open innovation is not a one-way process, but a mutual process.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the benefits of open innovation can outweigh the risks.
the benefits of openness are not limited to the open source software community, but that firms can also benefit from open development.
open innovation can be a very powerful tool for firms, but it requires a new mindset.
